Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 7 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1), R history (6). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 17 R code files for reproducibility and ran 3 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 12 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
  • 1 of 17 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce, 14 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 1 did not finish within the time limit.
  • 23 installable dependencies detected.

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to report data about people or animals that need an ethics statement, and lacked one.

Show details

The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, but we found no ethics statement. Such data need one: approval by an ethics committee, or a reason why none was needed. We based this on the sentences below. A paper can describe someone else’s study in the same words; if these data are not the authors’ own, no statement is needed.

We based this on:

Younger adults (n = 172; Mage = 23.7, SD = 3.8, range 18-35; 133 women, 39 men) and older adults (n = 174; Mage = 71.5, SD = 4.3, range 65-80; 97 women, 77 men) were recruited from the Zurich area (younger adults: university students; older adults: from the community).

16 US dollars) per hour, or, for students, partial course credit.

All participants provided written informed consent and were debriefed in the end.

To check Codebook Check

What we found

We found no codebook or README documentation for the 351 extracted data columns.

Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 68 codebook/README/label sources and 351 data columns across 32 files.

No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in CorrTable_Focus.csv. 2 column names appear more than once (worst: -0.05×2, 0.02×2), so 4 of the file’s 14 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

  • Duplicated column names in CorrTable_Baseline.csv. 2 column names appear more than once (worst: 0.28×2, 0.44×2), so 4 of the file’s 14 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 2 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 5 code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 2 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 24 distinct packages/libraries: blavaan, bmm, brms, circular, dplyr, gghalves, ggplot2, gtools, HDInterval, here, jsonlite, magick, pacman, parallel, patchwork, PupillometryR, rjson, rstudioapi, semTools, smartr, stringr, tidybayes, tidyverse, wesanderson. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

The repository holds MATLAB code. State the version of MATLAB used in the README, and list any add-ons the code needs (for Stata, the user-written commands installed with ssc install; for MATLAB, the toolboxes), so that readers can run the code with the same software.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We could not list every file of 1 repository, so the checks did not see all its files: https://osf.io/52sru/overview?view_only=03331344e3ba49e3b837ee20f203ae1c (could not be listed: the OSF API did not answer (HTTP 500)).
  • We classified 3111 files: 150 data, 1011 code, 349 documentation, 1529 materials, 72 unknown.
  • We found 57 tabular data files and extracted 157 columns from 16 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 65 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 18 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass local_path to point at a local copy.
  • Repository https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/Ambizione-IndividualDifferencesStudy exceeds the 500 MB per-repository budget: downloaded the smallest files up to the cap, 1 file omitted. Raise max_download_size to include more.
  • 23 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (Data/Int_ColCD_AggData.txt: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; Data/FB_ColCent_RawData.txt: 100% of columns are free text, not variables; Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 17 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 12 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

1 of 17 scripts ran to the end: 1 did not reproduce, 14 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 1 did not finish within our time limit.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script could not open a file, but the error does not say which.

  • change_background_color.R

Check every file the script reads. Make sure each one is in the deposit, and that its location is written from the top folder of the project.

A package could not be installed.

  • analysis_changedigitexp.R needs smartr.
  • analysis_colorperceptionexp.R needs smartr.
  • analysis_complex_span.R needs smartr.
  • analysis_digitexp.R needs smartr.
  • analysis_landoltexp.R needs smartr.
  • tasks/letter-judgement-changingSR/analysis_lettersexp.R needs smartr.
  • tasks/letter-judgement/analysis_lettersexp.R needs smartr.
  • tasks/perceptual-matching-color/analysis_perceptualmatching.R needs smartr.
  • tasks/perceptual-matching-luminance/analysis_perceptualmatching.R needs smartr.
  • analysis_registration.R needs smartr.
  • and 4 more

smartr is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/smartr”) or BiocManager::install(“smartr”), with the version you used.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • Analysis_AgeDifferences.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Other problems in the files

  • Analysis_AgeDifferences.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.
  • Descriptives_Plots&Table.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 17 R code files.

Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, source() call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

File paths

16 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: CFA_Baseline_4F.sem to SEM/CFA_Baseline_4F.sem (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); CFA_Baseline_3F.sem to SEM/CFA_Baseline_3F.sem (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); CFA_Baseline_Null.sem to SEM/CFA_Baseline_Null.sem (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Older.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Older.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Older_3F.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Older_3F.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Older_Null.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Older_Null.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Younger.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Younger.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Younger_3F.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Younger_3F.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); bCFA_Baseline_Younger_Null.RData to output/bCFA_Baseline_Younger_Null.RData (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R); CFA_FocusFX_4F.sem to SEM/CFA_FocusFX_4F.sem (in Analysis_AgeDifferences.R), and 6 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 48 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 6 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: color perception task_undefined.json, landolt gap processing task_undefined-4.json, number judgement task_undefined-2.json, perceptual_matching.json, color perception task_undefined (2).json, smiley processing task_undefined-2.json.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 17 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 1 timed out, 14 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

Dependency-unavailable errors

14 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

setwd() in the code

2 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): Descriptives_Plots&Table.R.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
Analysis_AgeDifferences.R 1 (non-literal)
Descriptives_Plots&Table.R 1 (non-literal)

Calls that install packages in the code

6 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Expand a row below to see the output each script produced.

> recolor_background = function(input_dir, output_dir, color, rename = FALSE) {
>   
>   if (require("magick") == FALSE) {
>     invisible(NULL)
>     library("magick")
>   }
>   
>   images = list.files(input_dir)
>

>

>     
>     # read the image
>     img = image_read(stringr::str_glue("{input_dir}/{images[i]}"))
>     
>     # Create a solid background image with the same dimensions and the new color
>     background = image_blank(image_info(img)$width, image_info(img)$height, color)
>     
>     # overlay the images to create a new image with the new background color:
>     img_new = image_composite(img, background)
>     
>     # specify file-name for new image

>

Readers without a MATLAB license cannot currently see what the code produced. Consider depositing the results as well, so they are visible without MATLAB installed: run diary('output.txt') (or diary on) before the analysis and diary off after to save a plain-text transcript of everything printed to the Command Window, or use publish('script.m', 'pdf') (or the Live Editor’s Export/Save As) to generate a single readable document with the code, its output, and any figures together.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

All detected t-tests and F-tests had an effect size reported in the same sentence.

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 2 matches under assumptions.
