Match = matching accuracy; WMCDE = delayed estimation; WMCPM = psychometric working memory capacity; Gf = fluid intelligence.

credible, r = .39, 95% CrI [.08, .61], BF10 = 8.12, confirming that WM maintenance retains unique Gf-predictive variance over and above Matching in older adults. In the reverse residual model -regressing Matching on WMCDE -the residual Matching-Gf correlation was r = .26, 95% CrI [.00, .50], with an inconclusive Bayes factor (BF01 = 0.43). Taken together, perceptual

Matching accounts for a larger share of WMC-related Gf variance in older than in younger adults, with WM maintenance contributing in addition to this perceptual baseline in both age groups. The residual path coefficients are illustrated in Figure 3.

Study 2 Method

Participants

Study 2 used data from a large study investigating cognitive processes underlying individual differences in cognitive abilities. 3 The study comprised a battery of 28 tasks distributed across three in-laboratory sessions of approximately 3.5 hours each; the perceptual matching tasks were administered in the second session, and the WMC battery and intelligence assessment in the third. Younger adults (N = 267; Mage = 23.0, SD = 3.6, range 18-35; 179 women, 80 men, 1 non-binary) were recruited via an online job market and mailing lists and received CHF 200 for the full study or partial course credit if they were students. All participants provided written informed consent.

3 None of the analyses reported in this manuscript have been previously published from this dataset. Courage and Frischkorn (2026) reported results on the relation between processing speed and WMC from the same dataset but using only partially overlapping tasks from the study.

Tasks and Procedure

Color Matching. On each trial, target and probe were presented simultaneously on white Study 2 Perceptual Matching Tasks. Color matching (A, B) and luminance matching (C, D) were each administered in two spatial arrangements: side-by-side (A, C), with target and adjustable probe shown as two horizontally separated stimuli, and concentric (B, D), with the probe at the center of a target ring. (A) Color matching: side-by-side (B) Color matching: concentric (C) Luminance matching: side-by-side (D) Luminance matching: concentric Note. On each trial, after a fixation cross (400-600 ms) the target and probe appeared simultaneously and remained visible until response. Participants first adjusted the probe to match the target by moving the cursor along the response wheel (color matching) or the linear response track (luminance matching) with no deadline on the matching response, then gave a confidence judgment, followed by an inter-trial interval (1,000-1,400 ms). The two configurations are contrasted in the Matching Configuration Comparison.

Color Delayed Estimation (WMCDE).

On each trial, an array of 2 or 4 colored dots was presented for 1,000 ms, followed by a 1,000 ms blank retention interval; at test, a probe dot indicated one randomly selected memory item and participants reproduced its color on the same continuous color wheel as in the matching task, without a response deadline (100 trials; 50 at each memory load). Performance was scored as reproduction accuracy [100 × (1 -mean angular error / 90°)], as in Study 1.

Working Memory Capacity (WMCPM).

We measured psychometric WMC with three

Fluid Intelligence (Gf).

We measured fluid intelligence with the Intelligence Structure Test (IST-5), a standardized, normed reasoning battery administered under fixed per-subtest time limits (Beauducel et al., 2024). Its verbal, numerical, and figural reasoning domain scores served as indicators of the latent Gf factor.

Statistical Analysis

The analytic approach followed Study 1 unless noted otherwise. Latent-variable SEMs were estimated with Bayesian estimation as in Study 1, with standardized latent variances and bifactor structures in which specific factors are orthogonal to the general factors: domain-specific factors for color and luminance matching, as in Study 1, and task-specific method factors for the four WMCPM task types (see below). To evaluate which tasks of the broader WMCPM battery captured most of the shared WMCPM variance compared to task-specific variance, we estimated the WMCPM factor with three parcels each from the complex span, letter updating, numerical updating, and color-binding tasks and introduced method factors for each task type (see the Supplementary Materials for detailed results). As in Study 1, three parcels each from the color and luminance matching tasks served as indicators of the Matching bifactor, with a domainspecific factor per feature domain; in the main model these parcels pooled trials across the sideby-side and concentric arrangements (a configuration-separated model is reported under

Matching Configuration Comparison).

The WMCDE factor also used three parcels aggregated across memory load as indicators. IST-5 verbal, numerical, and figural subtests served as indicators of the Gf factor. Parcels were formed and scored identically to Study 1 (cyclic everythird-trial assignment). Accuracy was scored as 100 × (1 -mean error / max error) for matching and WMCDE tasks; and percentage correct for WMCPM tasks. As in Study 1, all accuracy indicators were placed on the common 0-100 metric, which here keeps their variances comparable to the raw IST-5 subtest scores that index Gf.

We again estimated three models : (1) a correlation model with all factors freely correlated, (2) a residual model in which both the WMCDE and WMCPM factors were simultaneously regressed on Matching, yielding residual correlations with Gf after accounting for variance shared with Matching, and (3) the reverse residual model in which Matching was regressed on both WMCPM and WMCDE, as in Study 1.

Again, the proportional reduction in explained Gf variance 1 -(; ()* + /; , + ) was computed as in Study 1 as the primary outcome, with 95% CrIs from paired posterior draws, and Bayes factors for the incremental validity tests were computed as in Study 1.

As Study 2 included younger adults only, all models were estimated for the full sample.

To stabilize estimation, parallel-test constraints (equal loadings and error variances within each parcel bundle) were applied as in Study 1 and were likewise favored by approximate leave-oneout cross-validation (ΔLOOIC = -33). Therefore, the standardized loading reported below is identical across the three parcels of a factor.

Results

Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive performance is summarized in Table 2. Matching accuracy was high and near ceiling for both color and luminance features. Nonetheless, the latent Matching factor retained acceptable reliability (ωH = .75; see Figure 5). Side-by-side matching was more accurate than concentric matching, by less than 1 point for color and less than 3 points for luminance on the 0-100 scale (quantified in the Matching Configuration Comparison below); this small mean-level difference did not alter the Matching-Gf association. DE accuracy decreased with memory load, as expected, with wider individual variation at a memory load of four items.

Structural Equation Models

Correlation Model. In the correlation model, Matching predicted Gf substantially (r = .56, 95% CrI [.39, .71]), as did WMCPM (r = .81, 95% CrI [.68, .93]) and WMCDE (r = .60, 95% CrI [.45, .74]). Matching and WMCPM were substantially correlated (r = .45, 95% CrI [.33, .56]), consistent with a shared source of variance. Model fit was acceptable (PPP = .13, BCFI = .990, BRMSEA = .025, 95% CrI [.019, .031]; see Table S1). The full correlation model is illustrated in Figure 5. Note. Matching = perceptual matching accuracy (color and luminance); WMCDE = delayed estimation; WMCPM = psychometric working memory capacity (complex span, letter and number updating, color binding); Gf = fluid intelligence (IST-5). The 95% credible intervals of all displayed paths exclude zero.

Residual Models. We regressed both WMCDE and WMCPM on Matching. Matching accuracy explained 66% [43%, 86%] of WMCDE's zero-order Gf variance and 45% [27%, 63%] of WMCPM's zero-order Gf variance (posterior medians with 95% CrIs from paired posterior draws). Critically, both WMCDE and WMCPM credibly predicted Gf beyond Matching: the residual WMCDE-Gf was r = .35, 95% CrI [.19, .51], BF10 > 100; and the residual WMCPM-Gf was r = .59, 95% CrI [.44, .73], BF10 > 100.

concentric parcels load on two correlated Matching factors. The two factors correlated highly, r = .86, 95% CrI [.77, .92], and separating them did not credibly improve fit (Δelpd = -6.9 ± 5.3).

Each configuration predicted Gf substantially: r = .57, 95% CrI [.39, .73] for side-by-side and r = .48, 95% CrI [.30, .65] for concentric. The difference between them was small and not credible, Δr = .09, 95% CrI [-.06, .24], with BF01 = 4.05 favoring no difference. The Matching-Gf association therefore does not depend on the spatial arrangement of the stimuli.

Loadings on the Matching factor were comparable across configurations for colour (difference = .05, 95% CrI [-.01, .12]); for luminance the concentric arrangement loaded somewhat higher, though this difference was knife-edge: it excluded zero on the standardized scale but not the unstandardized one, so we treat it as uncertain rather than directional.

Luminance loadings were lower than colour loadings overall, as expected given that the luminance task contributed half as many trials.

Side-by-side matching was more accurate than concentric matching, for both colour (MSBS = 96.4, Mconc = 95.6; difference = 0.8 points, t(257) = 13.9, p < .001, dz = 0.86) and luminance (MSBS = 91.8, Mconc = 89.0; difference = 2.8 points, t(260) = 12.5, p < .001, dz = 0.77). 4 Because Matching accuracy was near ceiling with little between-person variance, these highly consistent within-person differences correspond to medium-to-large standardized effects despite small absolute magnitudes. This mean-level advantage did not, however, change the individual-differences structure. 4 This small accuracy cost likely has a perceptual rather than cognitive basis: in the concentric layout the target is a thin ring flanked by white (an inner mask and the background), whereas the side-by-side target is a solid patch. A surrounding field can shift the apparent lightness and color of an enclosed region, reflected in simultaneous lightness contrast and chromatic induction (Gilchrist et al., 1999; Shevell & Kingdom, 2008), which can add noise to the match and may contribute to the slightly larger cost we observed for luminance.

Proportional Reduction in Explained Gf Variance

Table 3 reports zero-order and residual latent correlations with Gf and the corresponding proportional reductions in explained variance. Matching accuracy accounted for a substantial and consistent share of both WMC factors' Gf-predictive variance across studies and age groups, with the largest reduction for WMCDE in older adults, despite the different WMCPM batteries used in Study 1 and Study 2. The reverse residual models complete this picture with a marked evidential asymmetry. WMCDE and WMCPM retained Gf-predictive variance beyond Matching in every group (smallest BF10 = 8.12), whereas Matching retained little credible Gf-predictive variance beyond its memory-enriched counterparts (WMCDE in Study 1; WMCPM and WMCDE jointly in Study 2; largest BF10 = 2.31), with inconclusive Bayes factors in all groups (Table 3, Matching rows, reports the corresponding proportional reductions). An order-restriction test supported the asymmetry predicted by our assumption that Matching variance is contained in WMCDE variance: the reduction of the Matching-Gf relation was credibly larger than the reduction of the WM factors' jointly explained Gf variance, in Study 1 younger adults (Δ = .46, 95% CrI [.02, .80], BForder = 48.37) and in Study 2 (Δ = .49, 95% CrI [.20, .75], BForder > 100). In older adults, where only WMCDE was available as a control, the same contrast was positive but inconclusive (Δ = .14, 95% CrI [-.32, .52], BForder = 2.55).

As all residual tests were performed at the latent level, where correlations are estimated free of attenuation by indicator unreliability, this asymmetry is not an artifact of differential measurement reliability.

General Discussion

We set out to decompose the WMC-Gf link into a component reflecting perceptual representation quality and a component specific to WM maintenance. Perceptual matching, which requires no memory maintenance, accounted for a substantial share of the covarianceroughly 60-73% of WMCDE's Gf-related variance and about 45% of that of WMCPM (Table 3).

The two residual tests were asymmetric: WM maintenance retained a credible Gf-predictive contribution beyond Matching in every group, whereas controlling for the memory factors (WMCDE in Study 1; both WM factors in Study 2) reduced the Matching-Gf relation, leaving the evidence for a residual link inconclusive in all groups. This pattern is consistent with Matching's

Gf-related variance being largely contained within that of WMC.

The maintenance-specific contribution to Gf held in both age groups, but perceptual matching accounted for a larger portion of WMCDE's Gf variance in older than younger adults.

This quantitative difference echoes the tightened coupling of sensory and intellectual functioning with adult age (Lindenberger & Baltes, 1994).

Perceptual Matching and the WMC-Gf Link

The association between perceptual matching and Gf has longstanding historical roots:

Galton (1883) proposed that sensory discrimination underlies general intelligence, Spearman (1904) could not confirm it convincingly with the methods of his era, but latent-variable studies later revived the conjecture (Deary et al., 2004). Our matching tasks extend this line: Matching accuracy predicted Gf substantially in younger adults (r = .52/.56) and strongly in older adults (r = .71), despite imposing no retention interval.

This shared variance is not specific to the visual domain or to any shared stimulus content. Matching-WMCPM correlations were r = .45 (Study 1, younger adults) and r = .45 (Study 2), even though the WMCPM tasks drew on spatial, verbal, and numerical content, and reasoning tests share no stimulus content with matching. A common limit on the fidelity of representations, rather than shared task content, most parsimoniously explains why a maintenance-free perceptual task covaries with both memory and reasoning. This is consistent with a global signal-to-noise ratio explaining general cognitive abilities (Oberauer et al., 2026) and with evidence that visual WM differences trace largely to a perceptual rather than mnemonic source (Pratte & Green, 2023).

The present results are consistent with a signal-to-noise account but do not constitute direct evidence for it. Behavioral Matching accuracy may also reflect motor noise, criterion setting, or strategic encoding, rather than a general signal-to-noise ratio. These alternatives, however, offer no explanation for the strong correlation of matching with WMC and Gf.

Still, the covariance pattern cannot say which aspect of the signal-to-noise ratio is shared: a common level of noise or shared variance in signal strength both produce the same correlational signature. Adjudicating between them requires an independent estimate of noise that does not depend on signal strength, which equivalent-noise paradigms provide (Lu & Dosher, 2008). The Supplementary Materials elaborate on the specific assumptions underlying the decomposition.

The Maintenance Account

Individual differences in WMC tasks are usually interpreted as differences in the capacity to maintain information. Yet, unlike research on constructs such as attentional control (Engle, 2002), which isolates attention-control variance from other task-required processes (Rey-Mermet et al., 2025; von Bastian et al., 2020), WMC research has rarely isolated maintenance-specific variance from other influences on performance. The present design comes closer: Because the matching and DE tasks differ only in the requirement to hold multiple items in WM, the DE residual after partialling out Matching estimates maintenance-specific variance. These residual correlations with Gf were credible across groups, indicating a maintenance-related contribution beyond perceptual precision.

How do these results relate to prior reports that WMC fully mediates the relationship between intelligence and sensory discrimination (Jastrzębski et al., 2021; Troche et al., 2014)?

Our reverse residual models put the same question to maintenance-free perceptual matching:

Matching retained no credible Gf variance beyond the memory factors (residual r = .17-.28, all Bayes factors inconclusive). This is what one should expect if WMC tasks require forming precise representations and maintaining them, whereas matching requires only the former: A mediator containing all of a predictor's Gf-relevant variance, plus more, must mediate it fully.

Full mediation therefore carries no information about which construct is more fundamental, and does not license the conclusion that perceptual precision plays no explanatory role for intelligence. Re-analysing the data of Jastrzębski et al. (2021) and Troche et al. (2014) (Supplementary Materials) reproduces this pattern; whether full mediation obtains depends on how broadly the mediator is measured. By the same standard, the asymmetry we report licenses no primacy claim for perceptual precision either.

The same logic applies to a related argument by Tsukahara et al. (2020). They reported that attentional control fully mediates the link between intelligence and sensory discrimination, whereas discrimination does not mediate the attentional-control-intelligence link. They interpreted this asymmetry as attention control being the more fundamental construct. If attention-control tasks depend on all the discrimination measures' Gf-related variance plus more, that mediation must occur without establishing causal priority. For Matching and DE, the experimental manipulation of the maintenance demand justifies the assumption that DE variance fully contains Matching variance; for discrimination and attention control we can only rely on plausibility. We find it plausible that perceptual precision contributes to every task involving stimulus discrimination, as all attention-control measures do, and less plausible that attention control matters in discrimination or matching tests, as they don't involve strong distractors or misleading response tendencies (Oberauer, 2024).

Implications for Theories of g

The present results are also relevant for accounts of the positive manifold underlying the g factor. Process Overlap Theory (POT, Kovacs & Conway, 2016) holds that g is not a causal entity but an emergent index of overlapping domain-general executive processes sampled by diverse tests. A task minimizing executive demands should then predict Gf only weakly. Yet our Matching -with no distractors, no conflicting goals, and no retention interval -predicted Gf substantially, and correlated sizably with WMC batteries drawing on spatial, verbal, and numerical content (r = .45 and .45), although POT predicts near-zero correlations between tests that share few executive processes. Accommodating this within POT requires assuming that Matching itself taps executive processes, stretching the concept until it becomes allencompassing. A signal-to-noise-ratio account offers a better explanation: A global limit on representational fidelity constraining perceptual encoding and WM maintenance alike would act as a genuine common cause of the positive manifold (Oberauer et al., 2026).

Limitations

Four limitations deserve acknowledgment. First, we cannot fully rule out a contribution of motivation to the Matching-Gf association; a motivation account would, however, have to explain why the least demanding task carries substantial variance shared with Gf. Plausible motivational effects on performance are modest: ≈ 9% of variance, from a motivationperformance correlation of r ≈ .30 (Gignac, 2018). Second, both samples are predominantly White, Swiss, and university-educated (a WEIRD population; Henrich et al., 2010), limiting generalization; the age comparison is cross-sectional, so age differences are confounded with cohort. Third, we examined perceptual precision only for visual features (color, orientation, and luminance); generalization to other domains remains open. Fourth, the analyses were not preregistered: the decomposition models were specified after data collection, making the model comparisons exploratory rather than confirmatory. The convergence of results across the two studies, rather than any single prespecified test, carries the evidential weight. The Supplementary Materials contain an extended discussion of each limitation.

Conclusion

A large part of the variance shared between WMC and Gf is also shared with a measure of perceptual precision that requires no memory maintenance and little, if any, attention control, a pattern that held across content domains and is consistent with a general signal-to-noise ratio limit on representational fidelity constraining cognition from perception to memory to reasoning.

At the same time, WM maintenance makes an additional contribution to fluid intelligence, providing stronger support than previous research to the hypothesis that the limited capacity of WM contributes to variance in intelligence.

SEM Fit Indices

For each study and age group we estimated three structurally equivalent latent models.

The correlation model freely estimates the latent correlations among the perceptual matching, delayed estimation, working-memory capacity, and intelligence factors. The residual model regresses delayed estimation (WMCDE) -and, where the design permits, WMCPM -on matching accuracy, isolating the variance these factors do not share with perceptual matching in the latent residuals (i.e., disturbances). The reverse residual model regresses matching on both WMCPM and delayed estimation (Study 1 younger adults, Study 2) or on delayed estimation alone (Study 1 older adults, where no separate WMCPM factor was identified), isolating the variance matching does not share with the WMC factors. Because the three models are algebraic reparameterisations of the same covariance structure, they have identical global fit; Table S1 therefore reports this shared fit once per group. All models fit the data well (BCFI ≥ .95, BRMSEA ≤ .06).

PPP = posterior predictive p value; BCFI/BTLI = Bayesian comparative fit index / Tucker-Lewis index; BRMSEA = Bayesian root mean square error of approximation (posterior median with 95% credible interval) (Garnier -Villarreal & Jorgensen, 2020). The correlation, residual, and reverse residual models share identical fit because they are mathematically equivalent reparameterisations of the same covariance structure. All models use parallel-test constraints (equal loadings and equal error variances within each parcel bundle), theoretically justified for random trial-split parcels and favored by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation over unconstrained variants in all three groups (ΔLOOIC = -23, -49, and -33 for S1 Younger, S1 Older, and S2, respectively; negative values favor the constrained model).

Measurement Invariance Across Age Groups

Because the primary Study 1 analyses report separate within-group structural models for younger and older adults, we tested whether the measurement model is invariant across age groups, using the standard configural → metric → scalar sequence, estimated with Bayesian multi-group CFA as in all other analyses (indicators z-scored on the combined sample, so that group differences in means and variances are preserved). Invariance steps were compared via the change in Bayesian fit indices and via approximate leave-one-out/WAIC cross-validation differences. The model specified one factor per task domain -color matching, orientation matching, color delayed estimation, and orientation delayed estimation -together with a fluidintelligence factor indicated by the three reasoning tests and the two WMCPM tasks. The WMCPM tasks are modelled as part of the Gf factor here because in older adults WMCPM and Gf are empirically inseparable (a separately estimated WMCPM factor yields a latent correlation above one and a non-positive-definite solution); a common, proper model across groups therefore requires WMCPM to load on Gf, as in the primary older-adult model.

Configural invariance held, with good fit in both groups (Table S2). Metric invariance was supported: constraining factor loadings to equality across groups did not meaningfully degrade fit (ΔBCFI = -.004) and slightly improved out-of-sample prediction (ΔLOOIC = -6).

Scalar invariance was not supported: additionally constraining indicator intercepts produced a substantial loss of fit (ΔBCFI = -.051; ΔLOOIC = +109; PPP < .01), indicating that some indicator intercepts differ between younger and older adults. We therefore report separate withingroup structural models rather than a constrained multi-group model. Because the latent correlations of interest are estimated within each age group, this partial scalar non-invariance -a difference in measurement intercepts (mean levels), not in loadings -does not bias the withingroup structural estimates.

Standardized Factor Loadings

The measurement model decomposes matching and DE into a general accuracy factor and domain-specific factors. For matching, a general Match factor loads on all colour-and orientation-matching parcels, while domain-specific MatC and MatO factors capture the residual variance specific to each feature domain; delayed estimation is modelled analogously (general DE plus domain-specific DeC and DeO). The WMCPM and Gf factors load directly on their task scores (WMC tasks and reasoning tests, respectively), without a parcel structure.

Each matching and DE task is split into three parcels by randomly partitioning its trials.

Because these parcels are drawn from the same pool of equivalent trials, they are treated as parallel measurements: Their loadings are constrained to be equal (tau-equivalence) and their residual variances are constrained to be equal (the parallel-test model). The three parcels in a bundle therefore receive identical estimates, so Table S3 reports a single representative loading per bundle rather than three redundant rows. All loadings are substantial, with 95% credible intervals excluding zero, supporting the adequacy of the measurement model.

Psychometric Working Memory Capacity Measurement Model

The Study 2 WMCPM battery was modelled as a nested-factor (bifactor) structure (Figure S4): a general WMCPM factor loading on all twelve parcels (three per task) of the four psychometric WM tasks, together with orthogonal task-specific factors for complex span, letter updating, and number updating, and a visual colour-binding factor (VisWMC) on the colourbinding parcels.

All four WMCPM tasks loaded substantially on the general WMCPM factor (colour binding β = .82, number updating β = .80, complex span β = .67, letter updating β = .55; all 95% CrIs exclude zero), consistent with a broad WMC construct cutting across paradigms and stimulus modalities (Schmiedek et al., 2009; Wilhelm et al., 2013). The general factor carried the large majority of the battery's reliable variance (ωH = .86), and each task-specific factor added a smaller reliable component (ωHS = .19-.47; Figure S4). Critically, the colour binding task, which involves no concurrent processing demands and measures purely the maintenance of visuospatial bindings, loaded as highly on the general WMCPM factor as the number updating task, suggesting that shared WMCPM variance is driven primarily by maintenance rather than by demands for managing simultaneous processing or updating outdated information (Frischkorn et al., 2022).

Robustness Check: Rank-Normalized Observed Variables

Accuracy parcel scores (computed as 100 × (1error ‾ /max_error)) are bounded on [0, 100] and positively skewed, because most participants perform well above chance on the matching and delayed estimation tasks. Because the Bayesian SEMs model the indicators with a normal likelihood, we re-ran the primary behavioral SEMs (correlation and residual models) after applying a rank-based inverse normal transformation to all perceptual task parcel scores (matching and delayed estimation parcels).

The rank-based inverse normal transformation (Blom, 1958) maps each variable to theoretical standard-normal quantiles via Φ !" [(, # -0.5)//], where , # is the rank of observation 1 and / is the sample size. This transformation preserves rank order and avoids the boundary problems of logit or arcsine transformations when scores are close to the bounds of the scale.

Note. Models use the same model syntax and Bayesian estimation as the primary analysis; only the observed parcel variables (matching and delayed estimation) are transformed prior to model fitting. Column abbreviations as in Table S1.

After rank normalization, the latent correlation between Matching accuracy and Gf was r = .51 (S1 Younger) and r = .71 (S1 Older), closely mirroring the untransformed estimates (r = .52 and r = .71, respectively). Matching accuracy continued to account for a comparable share of delayed estimation's Gf-predictive variance (rank-normalised proportional reduction: 63% in younger adults, 68% in older adults), consistent with the primary analysis and supporting the robustness of the main findings to violations of multivariate normality. This check also bears on a second concern: to the extent that matching accuracy approaches ceiling to different degrees in the two age groups, the raw accuracy scale could compress individual differences differentially across groups. Rank normalization removes any monotone distortion of the score scale, including ceiling compression, so the essentially unchanged latent correlations and proportional reductions indicate that the age-group pattern -including the stronger Matching-Gf association in older adults -is not an artifact of differential scale compression. A rank-normalisation robustness check was not conducted for Study 2, as the primary results showed no evidence of distributional problems in that sample.

Sensitivity Check: Older Adults with a Pure-Gf Factor

In the primary Study 1 models for older adults, WMCPM tasks (updating, spatial shortterm memory) load directly on the Gf factor alongside reasoning tests (letter sets, Raven, diagram reasoning), because the older-adult sample size does not support a separate four-factor model. This raises the concern that the high Matching-Gf correlation in older adults partially reflects shared WMC variance embedded in the Gf composite. To address this, we re-ran the correlation and residual models for older adults with a Gf factor restricted to the three reasoning tests only (letterset, raven, diagram); WMCPM tasks were excluded entirely from the model.

With the pure-Gf specification, the latent correlation between Matching accuracy and Gf in older adults was r = .69, 95% CrI [.49, .90], and the residual WMCDE-Gf path (r = .39, 95% CrI [.13, .60]) was consistent with the primary analysis. These results indicate that the strong Matching-Gf association in older adults is unlikely to be an artefact of loading WMCPM tasks on the Gf factor; the pattern holds when Gf is operationalised as reasoning tests only.

Conditions for the Decomposition Interpretation

The main text interprets the pattern of residual correlations as a variance decomposition Bayes factors are Savage-Dickey density ratios computed as in the main text (Wagenmakers et al., 2010), with the prior density at zero calibrated from prior-only samples of each model.

Conclusions were robust to flatter priors on the tested residual correlations (beta(1,1) and beta(2,2) in place of the primary beta(3,3)); the only value near a decision bound -the Study 2 WMCPM-only reverse residual -ranged from BF10 = 2.93 to 3.15 across priors, at the edge of the inconclusive band. At our studies' sample sizes, the attainable evidence for a true-zero residual is bounded by the width of the posterior (BF01 ≈ 5-6 at most), so moderate evidence is the strongest supportable description of the null results reported for our own data; the larger published samples reanalyzed in Reanalysis of Published Datasets below support correspondingly stronger bounds. Reanalysis of Published Datasets The containment account makes a prediction about other studies: Whether a construct X fully mediates the sensory discrimination-Gf relation should depend on how broadly the task battery for measuring X samples Gf-relevant processes. The share of the X-Gf covariance accounted for by discrimination should be substantial wherever discrimination and Gf are strongly related. We tested this in the publicly available person-level data of Jastrzębski et al. (2021) (https://osf.io/xp6g8/) and Tsukahara et al. (2020) (https://osf.io/hsqru/), fitting the same three structural models as in the main analyses (correlation, residual, and reverse residual; identical fit within each dataset) to each study and each controlled construct. The data of Troche et al. (2014) are not publicly available. Latent factors used the published person-level task scores as indicators (no parcels; specifications in scripts/lavaan/10_public_data_reanalysis.R): Gf from each study's reasoning tests; WM from the respective WM battery (Jastrzębski Study 1: complex and simple span, nback, mental counters, and change detection; Jastrzębski Study 2: complex and simple span, mental counters, and change detection; Tsukahara: the three complex span tasks); and attention control (AC) from Tsukahara's AC tasks (Study 1: antisaccade, flanker, and Stroop effects; Study 2: antisaccade, visual arrays, and sustained attention-to-cue). Sensory discrimination was modeled as a general discrimination factor over all discrimination tasks of each dataset -the closest available analogue of a general perceptual signal-to-noise index, corresponding to the general discrimination ability construct of Troche et al. (2014): for Jastrzębski's studies this was a second-order factor over task-family factors (Study 1: featural, numerosity, inspection time, and temporal; Study 2: featural visual, featural auditory, inspection time, temporal visual, and temporal auditory; memory and choice-RT tasks excluded), and for Tsukahara's studies it was a single factor over all threshold tasks (thresholds reverse-scored). Unlike our matching tasks, these batteries mix simultaneous with sequential or brief-exposure tasks, so the discrimination factors index perceptual precision broadly but are not maintenance-free control conditions.

Extended Discussion of Limitations

The following extends the brief limitations discussion in the main text.

Motivational confounds. Stable individual differences in motivation or effort could in principle generate spurious correlations among cognitive tasks if higher-motivated individuals consistently perform better across all measures. However, two features of the present data weigh against a strong motivational account. Structurally, an effort account would have to explain why the least demanding task (i.e. matching, with no WM demand) shows the strongest Gf correlation in older adults. Statistically, the plausible upper bound of motivation's influence can be estimated: the latent correlation between conscientiousness (a proxy for effortful engagement) and intelligence is approximately r ≈ .30 (Gignac, 2018), placing the maximum shared variance from motivation at roughly 9%, far less than the 45-73% of the WMC-Gf and DE-Gf covariance attributable to perceptual-matching accuracy in the present studies.

Construct validity of matching accuracy.

Although the matching task involves no WM retention interval, the accuracy score, computed from the mean angular reproduction error, aggregates multiple sources of variability beyond sensory signal-to-noise. Motor noise in the continuous adjustment response, response criterion-setting, occasional attentional lapses, and potentially strategic encoding of the target (e.g., verbally labeling a color) all contribute to matching error. These contributions are not WM maintenance processes, but they are also not exclusively reflections of the sensory signal-to-noise ratio. The present results therefore cannot constitute direct evidence for the signal-to-noise-ratio account of general intelligence; they are consistent with it. A further consequence is that the proportional reductions reported in the main text are lower bounds on the proportion of the WMC-Gf link that is shared with perceptual precision: To the extent that matching error contains Gf-irrelevant motor and criterion variance, the shared perceptual component is underestimated (see Conditions for the Decomposition Interpretation above). Future work using forced-choice discrimination tasks (which eliminate the motor adjustment component) or similarity judgment tasks (which do not depend on precise motor responses) will provide cleaner indices of perceptual precision.

Feature-space generalizability.

We examined continuous feature spaces: color hue and orientation (Study 1), and luminance (Study 2). The bifactor model in Study 2 supports domaingenerality across these three dimensions (variance in matching accuracy that cuts across color, luminance, and orientation predicts Gf), but it remains open whether equivalent patterns emerge for other continuous feature spaces (e.g., spatial frequency, motion direction, pitch, duration).

Task generalizability.

Perceptual matching (adjusting a continuous probe to match a target with no delay) is one operationalization of a maintenance-free perceptual task. Other zerodelay paradigms such as forced-choice discrimination (which stimulus is higher in contrast?) or simultaneous similarity judgment (how similar are these two colors?) eliminate the motor adjustment component and may yield purer estimates of perceptual discrimination. Whether these paradigms yield equivalent individual-difference structure is addressed in follow-up work in our lab. The matching paradigm also requires sustained encoding of the target while the probe is adjusted; gaze shifts between target and probe could recruit brief iconic storage, and whether this constitutes a form of early WM is debated (Pratte & Green, 2023). Study 2's concentric arrangement was designed to minimize such gaze shifts by placing the probe at the center of the target ring: matching accuracy was slightly lower in this arrangement, and its correlation with Gf did not credibly differ from the side-by-side arrangement (see the Matching Configuration Comparison in the main text), indicating that gaze-mediated iconic storage is unlikely to carry the association between matching and Gf.

SEM Indicator Intercorrelations

Before fitting the latent models, we examined the raw correlational structure among the observed indicators. Figures S1-S3 display the zero-order Pearson correlations for each sample.

In every panel the lower triangle encodes each correlation as a shaded ellipse -narrower and more saturated ellipses denote stronger associations, with blue indicating positive and red negative correlations -and the upper triangle gives the same coefficients numerically. Parcelled indicators (matching and delayed estimation) are shown as bundle means across their three random trial-splits, so that each task contributes a single column.

Two features of these matrices motivate the structural models. First, the indicators form a positive manifold: with negligible exceptions, all correlations are positive. Second, the perceptual matching indicators (MatC, MatO, MatL) correlate not only with the delayedestimation and working-memory indicators but also with the fluid-intelligence indicators. This is the raw-data pattern that the latent models subsequently formalise and disattenuate for measurement error, allowing the perceptual and maintenance contributions to the WMC-Gf relationship to be partitioned. the covariance of Gf with other constructs: 68% and 38% of the WM-Gf covariance in Jastrzębski's Studies 1 and 2, 81% and 50% of the WMC-Gf covariance in Tsukahara's Studies 1 and 2, and 92% and 66% of their AC-Gf covariance -bracketing the correlations between Gf and perceptual matching in our studies. Second, whether or not a mediating construct (WMC or AC) fully mediated the link between sensory discrimination and Gf depended on how broad the test battery for measuring the mediating construct was. Full mediation was obtained with Jastrzębski's WM batteries (in their Study 2 the residual was nominally negative, r = -.23, 95% CrI [-.48, -.02], indicating no positive unique path from discrimination to Gf) and with Tsukahara's AC factors. By contrast, sensory discrimination retained clear unique variance beyond a WMC factor formed from the three complex span tasks in both of Tsukahara's studies (r = .32 and .33, BF10 > 100 in both). We argue that this is a consequence of the relatively narrow measurement of WMC through only one task paradigm -complex span batteries do not exhaust the shared variance between Gf and sensory discrimination. Two qualifications apply:

First, battery breadth was not operationalized independently of these outcomes, and broader batteries also contain more indicators, so higher reliability of the mediating factor is an alternative explanation that these analyses cannot rule out. Second, these reanalyses are descriptive and use simplified measurement models; they are reported to illustrate that the decomposition question and the mediation question give different answers in the same data, not as re-estimates of the original studies' models. One final observation: In Tsukahara's Study 1, the link between Gf and AC was largely mediated by sensory discrimination (proportional reduction 92%; residual r = .21, BF10 = 1.61, inconclusive). Applying the same mediation logic that these authors used to declare AC the causally fundamental construct would, in light of this result, have crowned sensory discrimination as the more fundamental construct. Colors were drawn from a continuous wheel in CIELAB space centered at L* = 70, a* = 20, b* = 38 with a chromatic radius of 60, identical to the color wheel used in Study 1. Participants adjusted the probe color by moving the mouse cursor along the outer color wheel until a mouse click confirmed the selection, followed by a confidence judgment (40 trials per condition, 80 total). Confidence judgments were collected as part of the broader study protocol and are not analyzed here. Luminance Matching. On each trial, target and probe gray patches were presented simultaneously in side-by-side or concentric arrangement, with gray levels spanning 10-90 on a 0-100 lightness scale. Participants adjusted the probe's grayscale value by moving the mouse cursor along a linear response track below the stimuli until a mouse click confirmed the match, followed by a confidence judgment (20 trials per condition, 40 total). Performance was scored on the same 0-100 accuracy scale as color matching [100 × (1 -mean error / max error)], with deviation computed on the response scale. The trial sequence and the two spatial arrangements are illustrated in Figure 4.

Figure 4

Figure4 verbal/numerical tasks and one visual binding task.

In the Number Complex Span task, participants selected the larger of two two-digit numbers on each of 4 steps (2,000 ms per comparison) while memorizing the number indicated by a directional arrow after each selection, then serially recalled all 4 memorized numbers at test (12 trials; scored as percentage recalled in order). In the Letter Updating task, participants encoded 4 color-letter bindings, updated 2 of them by replacing the bound letter with a new one, then recalled the current letter for each color via a response matrix (1,500 ms per encoded and updated item; 10-s recall deadline; 15 trials; scored as percentage of correctly recalled final letters). In the Number Updating task, participants encoded 4-5 digits at distinct grid locations in a 4 × 4 grid, applied three successive arithmetic operations per trial, each to a randomly selected digit, so that some digits were updated more than once and others not at all (+1, +2, -1, or -2; 1,000 ms per encoding, update, and retention interval), and recalled the final digit at each location by key press (16 trials; scored as percentage correct). In the Color Binding task, participants encoded the color and location of 4-5 items presented one at a time in a 4 × 4 grid (1,000 ms per item; 1,000 ms retention), then recalled either the color at a probed location or the location of a probed color via cued recall (16 trials; scored as percentage correct).

in the notation of the Statistical Analysis of Study 1, Var(WMC $% ) = Var(9) + Var(;) + Var(< $% ) and Var(Match) = Var(9) + Var(< &'()* ), with9 = precision of perceptual encoding and ; = maintenance: WMCDE tasks reflect representational quality and maintenance, whereas matching reflects chiefly representational quality, so matching's Gf-relevant variance should be (nearly) contained within that of WMCDE. Under this containment structure, full mediation of the Matching-Gf relation by the WMCDE factor is the expected outcome, and it carries no information about which construct is more fundamental. This interpretation rests on assumptions that deserve explicit statement: 1. Common signal dimension. The perceptual precision captured by matching and the perceptual component of WMC task performance reflect the same latent dimension. For WMCDE, which uses the same stimuli and response format as matching, this holds by design even if precision were feature-specific; for WMCPM it additionally requires perceptual precision to generalize across content domains. 2. Gf-irrelevant task-specific variance. Matching-specific variance -motor adjustment noise, criterion setting, encoding strategies -is unrelated to Gf. If part of it predicted Gf, matching would retain unique Gf variance beyond WMCDE. 3. Latent-level testing. The residual tests are performed on latent variables. With fallible manifest scores, unreliability of the WMCDE measures alone would produce apparent partial mediation. 4. No suppression. Regressing matching on the WMC factors does not induce suppression between maintenance variance and matching-specific variance. The observed residual correlations are all positive, showing no suppression signature. 5. Additivity. Representational quality and maintenance combine approximately additively in producing Gf variance; strong interactive combinations could produce patterns the decomposition would misattribute. Under these assumptions the decomposition makes a falsifiable joint prediction: WMCPM and WMCDE should retain Gf-relevant variance beyond Matching, whereas Matching should retain no Gf-predictive variance beyond the WMC factors. The first half was supported decisively in every group (smallest BF10 = 8.12). The second half was not decisively supported in any group: the Bayes factors were inconclusive in Study 1 younger adults (BF01 = 0.64), Study 1 older adults (BF01 = 0.43), and Study 2 (BF01 = 1.07, residual r = .17, 95% CrI [.01, .33]); in no specification did evidence for absence reach moderate strength (largest BF01 = 1.89; see below). A decisively positive matching residual (BF10 > 3) would have refuted strict containment; the observed residuals were small and their Bayes factors inconclusive, though their 95% CrIs lie mostly above zero -leaving open a small unique matching contribution. Controlling for WMCDE alone in Study 2 indeed left a credible residual (see below). We therefore describe the structure as approximate rather than strict containment.Alternative parameterizations of the reverse model. The reverse residual test can regress Matching on WMCDE, on WMCPM, or on both jointly. The main text controls matching for WMCDE -its maintenance-enriched counterpart -in both Study 1 age groups, and for WMCPM and WMCDE jointly in Study 2, where the two memory factors are separable (latent r = .59); in Study 1 younger adults they are strongly correlated (latent r = .84), so the joint regression weights are not interpretable there -though the residual Matching-Gf correlation, the quantity of interest, remains so. The two WMCPM-based variants for Study 1 younger adults yield the same conclusion: regressing Matching on WMCPM alone -the latent-variable analogue of the prior WMC-only mediation tests(Jastrzębski et al., 2021; Troche et al., 2014) -gives a residual Matching-Gf correlation of r = .19 (BF01 = 1.89), and the two-predictor model gives r = .19 (BF01 = 1.84), both inconclusive. In Study 2, the single-predictor WMCPM model gives r = .21 (BF10 = 3.31), close to the two-predictor estimate, at the boundary of the inconclusive band.Controlling for WMCDE alone in Study 2, in contrast, leaves a clearly credible residual: r = .29, 95% CrI [.12, .46], BF10 = 22.38. The single colour DE task does not fully account for the shared variance of Gf with the two matching tasks (color and luminance matching), whereas Study 1's DE factor -which spans the same feature spaces as Matching (colour and orientation) -leaves only an inconclusive residual. This result should not surprise us: Mediation is expected to be complete only when the set of DE tasks samples the perceptual variance of Matching at least as broadly as the Matching tasks themselves. The quantity of interest -the residual Matching-Gf covariance -is an algebraic function of the latent correlations and is stable across parameterizations that control the same factors. Robustness transfer. The correlation, residual, and reverse residual models are reparameterisations of the same covariance structure, so the reverse-model semipartial is an algebraic function of the latent correlations among Matching, the WMC factors, and Gf. The robustness of these correlations to rank-normalisation (Robustness Check: Rank-Normalized Observed Variables) and to the pure-Gf specification (Sensitivity Check: Older Adults with a Pure-Gf Factor) therefore extends to the reverse residual correlations without re-fitting.
